memo:
The $112.1 million shortfall is shared across stakeholders, with the least harm to customers, the environment and future products.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit on lower prices at the coming year's volume. Suppliers keep their volume, though they take a real price cut.

Customers bear nothing. A price increase in a downturn risks losing the unit volume that the lower revenue already reflects, and the board's aim is value for customers too.

Research and development and environmental projects are untouched. Cutting R&D would damage future products and the engineering staff, and cutting environmental projects would fall on the communities near the plants. Both are small enough to protect.

The workforce bears $30.0 million: $10.0 million through a modest wage and hours reduction, well inside the 10% limit, and $20.0 million through eliminating roles, concentrated in management, business and financial operations and office support rather than in the plants. Plant production, maintenance and warehouse headcount is kept, because the plants will need those people when orders recover and retraining costs $15,000 per person. Severance on the eliminated roles is a one-off cash cost I accept.

Shareholders bear the largest remaining share, $74.4 million of lower operating income. Dividends and buybacks are a board decision, and I recommend the board consider reducing repurchases first, since they absorb cash the Company can use to protect its balance sheet through the downturn. Debt to EBITDA is 2.30 times today, and the undrawn $300 million facility gives room if the downturn runs longer than planned.

This split protects the plants and the engineering base, keeps suppliers and customers whole in volume, and asks shareholders for the largest share.

I have decided to cover the $112.1 million shortfall without eliminating any roles, cutting research and development, or reducing environmental projects. The allocation is: shareholders bear $74.4 million through lower operating income; customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase of about 1.3%, well inside the 3.5% they would accept, because a smaller increase is more likely to protect volume in a downturn; suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiated saving available on renewals; and the workforce bears $10.0 million through a modest cut in wages or hours, shared across all staff and well under the 10% cap. The workforce keeps its roles, which avoids severance costs, preserves plant knowledge and skills that would be expensive to rebuild in the recovery, and avoids the community harm of plant job losses. Engineering capacity and future products are protected, since the research and development budget is untouched. Environmental projects continue, protecting air and water improvements near the plants. The main cost falls on shareholders, which I consider justified: the Company earns $162.4 million net, generates $166.5 million of free cash flow, and has $300 million of undrawn credit, so it can absorb a lower profit year without strain to its debt position. The board may wish to revisit the payout level, which currently absorbs 90% of net income, as a separate decision, since payouts do not change operating income. I will review this allocation at each quarter's results and move toward role or wage actions only if volumes fail to recover.

The coming year's shortfall is $112.1 million, from a 15% fall in volume. I chose to spread it across shareholders, suppliers and the workforce, and to protect customers, the environment and future products.

No roles are eliminated. Job cuts would add severance paid from cash, fall hardest on plant staff whose pay is already modest, and would weaken the Company's capacity to recover when orders return. Keeping people in place is the choice that best serves employees and the communities around the plants.

The workforce bears $24.4 million through a 10.0% reduction in wages or hours, the full cap, which applies because no roles are removed. This is a real cost to employees and I will try to keep it temporary, reviewing it each quarter.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million from renegotiating renewals, the full cap on the lower volume. The Company pays suppliers in an average of 72 days, so I will not seek payment-term changes that would strain smaller suppliers.

Customers bear nothing extra. Raising prices in a downturn would deepen the demand problem for them, and the sales estimate of acceptable increases is only useful if orders are stable.

Research and development and environmental projects are untouched at $30.0 million and $4.5 million. Cutting either would hurt future products or the communities near our plants for a modest saving.

Shareholders absorb the remaining $80.0 million through lower operating income. The Company's cash above its minimum, its undrawn facility, and its free cash flow give room for this. Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision and I recommend the board review them against the lower earnings.

We are closing a $112.1 million operating income gap from a 15% volume decline. I have chosen to protect people, the environment, future products and customers as far as possible, and to let shareholders absorb the largest share.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full amount obtainable on the 30% of spend renewing next year. This is a negotiated reduction on contracts that come up anyway, so it does not disrupt supply.

The workforce bears $24.4 million through a 10% cut in wages or hours, the maximum allowed. I chose this over eliminating roles. Our plants hired 500 people last year and retraining takes about six months, so laying off skilled machinists, welders and technicians now would destroy capability we will need when volumes return. No roles are eliminated, so no severance is paid and the full wage measure is available. The reduction should be time-limited, with a stated commitment to restore pay and hours as volumes recover, and I will ask the board to review it quarterly.

Shareholders bear $80.0 million of lower operating income. That is a large hit, and I recognize it falls on the owners who have funded the Company. But shareholders are the only stakeholder group that can absorb a cut without losing jobs, training or the plants' ability to serve customers. The board should note that this reduces the cash available for payouts, which I recommend be reviewed alongside the dividend and repurchase program.

Customers bear nothing: we will not raise prices into a downturn. Environmental projects, compliance and research and development are fully protected. Cutting R&D would weaken products we need for recovery, and environmental projects serve nearby communities. Debt stays unchanged, and liquidity remains adequate, with the undrawn facility available.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income, and I have chosen to spread that shortfall across stakeholders rather than place it on any one group.

I have kept every role in place. Eliminating roles would fall on a workforce of 3,310 whose average pay is $73,820, add severance costs paid from cash, and damage the capability we will need when volume returns, including the skilled machinists, welders and assemblers we spent this year recruiting and training. Protecting jobs is the choice that most preserves value for employees and the communities around our six plants.

Customers bear $30.0 million through price increases. The sales organization judges up to 3.5% acceptable, worth $52.5 million, but in a downturn I have set a more moderate increase so that we do not lose volume to competitors and distributors. This is below the $44.6 million cap for that reason.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiated saving available. We will press for it on the 30% of spend renewing next year, while paying on existing terms, so that we do not strain the suppliers who supply us through a downturn.

Workers bear $15.0 million through a limited reduction in wages or hours, below the 10% ceiling. This is a real cost to employees, and I accept it reluctantly in place of layoffs.

Research and development is cut by $10.0 million, protecting the core of the product and controls roadmap for future customers and our engineers. The environmental projects budget is left untouched at $4.5 million, so energy-efficiency and emissions work near our plants continues.

Shareholders bear the remaining $49.4 million as lower operating income. The Company's balance sheet, with debt to EBITDA of 2.30 times, cash above the minimum, and a $300 million undrawn facility, can absorb this. The board should review its payout policy, which currently exceeds net income, in light of the lower profit expected next year.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that no single stakeholder bears it alone and the parts that reach people closest to production, communities and future products are protected.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating agreements coming up for renewal. This is a moderate ask given that suppliers also face the downturn, and we keep payment terms and relationships intact.

Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase of roughly 1.6%, well below the 3.5% ceiling. In a downturn, a full increase risks volume we cannot afford to lose, so we take a measured step.

The workforce bears $40.0 million through eliminated roles, concentrated in management, business and financial operations, and office and administrative support, rather than in plant production, maintenance or field service. This preserves the capacity of the people who build and service machines, and avoids cutting wages or hours. The severance cost, paid from cash, is a one-time charge we will plan for. We will also use attrition and the non-replacement of open roles first, and redeploy people where possible, since the plants recently hired 500 people from outside and retraining is a known path.

Shareholders bear the remaining $44.4 million as lower operating income. This is a significant ask, but it is less than 40% of the shortfall and keeps our balance sheet within policy.

We protect environmental projects and research and development entirely. Those budgets fund energy efficiency, emissions reduction and the products and controls that will matter when demand recovers. Cutting them would transfer cost to communities and to our future.

Plant 6, which is loss-making, should be reviewed separately over the coming quarters.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I have allocated it so that the people who depend on the Company bear as little as possible, and so that the burden falls mainly on shareholders, who hold the residual claim.

Shareholders bear $84.4 million through lower operating income. This is the largest share because shareholders receive the residual and the board's payout policy already distributes 90% of net income. Their dividends and repurchases should be reviewed against the lower profit, and I recommend the board consider this before approving the full $146.1 million.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit of negotiated price reductions on the lower volume. Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase, deliberately set below the 3.5% that the sales organization believes customers would accept without losing volume. This reduces the risk of losing orders in a downturn, which would damage the Company and its suppliers more than a smaller price rise would.

I have not eliminated any roles, so there is no severance cost from cash and no loss of jobs for the 3,310 employees. I have not cut wages or hours. R&D is kept at $30.0 million to protect future products and the engineering staff, and environmental projects are kept at $4.5 million to protect emissions reductions and waste reduction near the plants.

The main risk is that the operating margin falls sharply, and that the Company may need to draw on the $300.0 million undrawn facility or use excess cash if payouts continue at current levels. Debt to EBITDA would rise from 2.30 times as EBITDA falls. The board should monitor leverage and revisit this allocation quarterly as orders become clearer.

The downturn cuts operating income by $112.1M. I have decided to spread that shortfall across the parties best able to absorb it, and to protect the workforce, future products and the environment where possible.

Raising prices by the full 3.5% the sales organization says customers will accept ($44.6M) is the largest single contributor. It is a real cost to customers, but it is the one that leaves the Company's capability intact. Negotiating lower supplier prices on the 30% of spending coming up for renewal ($7.7M) asks suppliers to share the burden at a modest 4% on those contracts, well inside the purchasing estimate.

I chose not to eliminate any roles and not to cut wages or hours. Eliminating roles would cost severance from cash and fall on 1,900 plant workers and 1,410 other employees who have already seen a difficult year; a 10% pay cut would hit every employee's payroll. I also made no cut to research and development, which protects new models and the controls software customers rely on, and no cut to environmental projects, which protects energy-efficiency and emissions work that benefits nearby communities.

The remaining $59.8M is accepted as lower operating income, borne by shareholders. The Company's balance sheet supports this: debt is 2.3 times EBITDA, interest cover is 7.4 times, and $444.9M of liquidity is available. Net income will fall, and the board may wish to review the 90% combined payout of dividends and repurchases in light of the downturn, since that decision sits outside this allocation.

I will monitor the volume outlook quarterly. If the decline deepens, the wages-and-hours and workforce levers remain available, and I would recommend reviewing them before the cuts to R&D or environmental projects.

The $112.1M shortfall is a volume downturn, not a cost problem, so I looked first at what protects the people and places the Company depends on. I raise no prices: customers are already cutting orders, and a price rise into falling demand would likely cost more volume than it recovers. I cut no R&D, because it funds the product line the Company needs after the downturn, and I make no across-the-board pay or hours cut, because that spreads hardship over the whole workforce, including the plant staff who are hardest to replace.

I take the full discretionary environmental budget ($4.5M). Permit-required compliance spending of $3.0M stays, so air, water and waste obligations are still met, but the energy-efficiency and emissions projects pause for a year. I take $7.7M from suppliers through renegotiation at renewal, which is the full available saving on contracts coming up.

Eliminating roles is $45.0M, concentrated in non-plant overhead rather than production, so the trained plant workforce and its retraining cost are preserved. This still means real job losses, and severance will be paid from cash, which I accept as the cost of protecting the plants. Shareholders bear the remaining $54.9M through lower operating income. Dividends and buybacks are for the board to set; I recommend the board review them given this earnings reduction, but that decision sits outside this allocation.

The allocation spreads the burden across suppliers, the environment budget, the workforce and shareholders, and it leaves customers and the Company's future products largely untouched. Plant 6 remains a loss-maker and should be reviewed separately, with the board considering its long-term footprint once volumes recover.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall across stakeholders in proportion to their capacity to absorb it, and I have protected the assets the Company needs to recover.

Customers: I am raising prices by $20.0 million, about 1.6%, well below the 3.5% ceiling. Customers are themselves under pressure in this downturn, and a smaller increase protects unit volume and the relationships we will need when orders return.

Suppliers: I am negotiating the full $7.7 million available on contracts up for renewal. This is a real but bounded ask. Suppliers share the downturn, and I have kept it at the level purchasing judges achievable without straining supply.

Workforce: I am eliminating $40.0 million of roles, concentrated in management and non-plant functions, and cutting wages and hours by $10.0 million on the remaining payroll, well under its cap. I have deliberately not touched plant staff: we hired 500 plant workers last year at real cost, and retraining replacements takes six months and $15,000 each. Severance will be paid from cash.

Future and environment: I am making no cut to research and development or environmental projects. Cutting R&D would weaken products we need for recovery, and environmental projects are the commitments communities near our plants depend on.

Shareholders: I am absorbing $34.4 million through lower operating income. Shareholders are the residual claimants, and the balance sheet can carry it: debt to EBITDA is 2.3 times, we have $44.1 million of cash above minimum, and the $300 million facility is undrawn. Payouts are not part of this decision and are for the board to set separately.

The total is exactly $112.1 million. I recommend the board review the workforce actions again at the next quarter.

We must absorb a $112.1 million operating income shortfall from a 15% volume decline. I have chosen to spread it so that no single stakeholder bears a disproportionate or lasting harm.

Shareholders bear $100.0 million as lower operating income. This is the largest share because shareholders can absorb it most easily: the Company paid $146.1 million in dividends and repurchases last year against $166.5 million of free cash flow, has 2.3 times debt to EBITDA, $444.9 million of liquidity, and $44.1 million of cash above its operating minimum. The board can reduce repurchases, which it sets separately, to protect the balance sheet without touching jobs, customers or the environment.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on renewing agreements. This is the full available amount on the reduced volume. It is a meaningful ask, but a downturn that cuts their volume also gives the Company leverage, and we will negotiate fairly on terms and payment timing.

The workforce bears $4.4 million through a modest reduction in wages or hours, about 1.8% of the remaining payroll. I have not eliminated any roles. Our plants hired 500 people last year and the Company has a retraining path, but layoffs would cost jobs and severance during a downturn and would make the recovery harder. A small, shared reduction is preferable to cutting people.

I am not raising prices: customers are already facing a downturn, and a price rise would risk losing the volume we need. I am not cutting environmental projects ($4.5 million) or research and development ($30.0 million): these protect the communities near our plants and our future products and engineering staff, which matter for long-term value.

Plant 6, which lost $9.0 million, should be reviewed separately for its fixed-cost structure, but this decision does not depend on that review. We will report progress quarterly against these allocations.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall across six lines, leaving the plant workforce, R&D and environmental projects largely intact.

Prices: $20.0 million from customers, a moderate increase well below the 3.5% ceiling. Customers have absorbed increases for three years and volume is already falling, so I kept this deliberately below the maximum.

Suppliers: $7.7 million, the full available saving. Suppliers are also exposed to the downturn, so this is a firm but achievable ask, and it is the largest realistic saving available.

Roles: $50.0 million of roles eliminated, weighted toward management, office and administrative support, business and financial operations, and sales overhead rather than production and maintenance. The Company hired 500 plant workers last year and will need skilled machinists, welders and field technicians when volume returns; cutting them now would be costly to rebuild. Severance on this amount is a one-time cash cost that the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum and the $300 million undrawn facility can cover.

Shareholders: $34.4 million accepted as lower operating income. Given the 90% payout ratio, the board may wish to review payouts, which are outside this decision.

Not used: R&D (protects future products and engineering staff), wages and hours (protects the workforce), and environmental projects (protects communities and permitted-plus-discretionary commitments).

Trade-off: the plant workforce bears the least, but the overhead reduction is real and affects people. I recommend monitoring Plant 6, which is loss-making, as a candidate for further action if the downturn lasts beyond the coming year.

We must close a $112.1 million operating-income gap on a 15% volume decline. I have spread it across stakeholders rather than loading it on one group.

Workforce: I am eliminating $70.0 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in management, office and administrative, business and financial operations, and non-plant roles, with attrition used first. Plant staff are protected where possible, because the plants hired 500 people last year and retraining a plant worker costs $15,000 each, so redeploying people is cheaper than rehiring later. Severance (about $6 to $9 million) will be paid from cash, which is above the minimum operating level. I am not cutting wages or hours: a 10% pay cut would fall hardest on the lowest paid and erode the skills we need for recovery.

Suppliers: we will take the full $7.7 million from renewals on the 30% of spend coming up. This is a fair ask in a downturn and the Company still pays on 72-day terms.

Customers: a modest $15.0 million price increase, about 1.2%, well inside the 3.5% customers would accept, to limit the risk of losing volume at a weak time.

Future and environment: I am not cutting R&D ($30.0 million), which protects new products and engineering jobs, nor the $4.5 million environmental projects that reduce emissions and landfill waste.

Shareholders: $19.4 million of lower operating income. Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision; I recommend the board review them given that payouts were 90% of net income last year.

This keeps leverage manageable and preserves capacity to recover when volumes return.

I have decided to absorb the $112.1 million shortfall without eliminating any roles. Protecting 3,310 jobs is the priority in a downturn: eliminating roles would cost up to $309.8 million of payroll and benefits, plus severance paid from cash, and would fall hardest on plant staff whose average pay is about $55,000.

The decision draws on four sources. First, I am taking the full $7.7 million supplier saving. Suppliers bear this through renegotiated prices on the 30% of spend coming up for renewal, a modest ask in a year when our volumes are falling. Second, I am cutting wages and hours by $12.0 million, about 4.9% of the remaining payroll. This is well below the 10% ceiling and is a shared sacrifice that keeps everyone employed. Third, I am not raising prices: customers are already facing a downturn, and a price increase would weaken our relationships and future orders. Fourth, I am leaving R&D and environmental projects untouched. Cutting R&D would damage future products and the engineering team, and environmental projects protect the communities near our plants.

The remaining $92.4 million falls on shareholders as lower operating income. This is the stakeholder best placed to absorb a cyclical decline, and the board's payout decision is separate from this one. I am aware the wage and hours reduction is a real cost to employees, and I would revisit it if the downturn deepens or recovers early. I will monitor the plants closely, particularly Plant 6, which is already loss-making, and report back on whether further structural action is warranted.

I have spread the $112.1 million shortfall across the stakeholders who can best absorb it, and I have protected the future and the community.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a price increase of 3.5%, the largest increase the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume. It matches the increase they absorbed last year and does not require any new burden on them.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on the 30% of supply agreements coming up for renewal. The 4.0% reduction is the purchasing department's estimate of what is obtainable, and it is shared with suppliers across a broad base.

The workforce bears $42.0 million in total. Eliminating $32.0 million of roles, measured at payroll and benefits, is concentrated in management, business and financial operations, and office and administrative roles, and the one-time severance cost is paid from cash. Plant production and maintenance staff are kept wherever possible. A 10.0%-capped reduction in wages or hours of $10.0 million, applied to the payroll that remains, is a shared, temporary sacrifice, and it sits below the $21.2 million cap that remains after the roles are removed.

Shareholders bear $17.8 million through lower operating income. This is the residual after the other lines, and it is the smallest tolerable share, since cutting dividends and repurchases is a separate board decision.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. Both protect the Company's future products, its engineering staff and the communities near its plants, and cutting them would move cost onto those stakeholders over the longer term.

I will monitor volume each quarter and revisit the allocation if the downturn deepens or recovers faster than expected.

I have decided to close the $112.1 million shortfall mainly by accepting lower operating income, with smaller shares borne by suppliers and the workforce, and nothing borne by customers, the environment, or future products.

Shareholders bear $92.4 million. The Company can absorb this: it holds $44.1 million of cash above its operating minimum, has a $300 million undrawn revolver, and its payout policy is a separate board lever that can be reviewed. I am not asking shareholders to bear the whole gap, but they carry the largest share because it is the least harmful to people in a downturn.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating the 30% of spend coming up for renewal. Suppliers are also facing lower volumes, so this should be negotiated fairly, with the aim of preserving the supply relationships we need when orders recover.

The workforce bears $12.0 million through a modest reduction in wages or hours, about 4.9% of payroll. I have chosen this over eliminating roles. Layoffs would bring severance costs of several million dollars, and the Company would lose skilled production and maintenance staff it would need to rehire and retrain when volume returns. Pay reductions are spread across all employees and can be reversed.

I have not raised prices, since customers are already cutting orders and a price increase could deepen the volume loss. I have not cut environmental projects, which protect the communities near our plants, nor research and development, which protects future products and engineering staff.

The main risk is that Plant 6, already loss-making, and the lower-margin plants remain under pressure. I will ask the board to review plant footprint in the next quarter if volumes stay below plan.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across the stakeholders who can best absorb it, and to avoid placing the burden on the workforce's jobs, future products, or the environment.

Prices (customers), $30.0 million: The sales team estimates customers would accept up to 3.5%, worth $52.5 million, but in a downturn a price rise that costs volume would undo its benefit. I have taken a moderate increase of about 2.0% on the lower revenue base, below the $44.6 million ceiling, to leave room for customers to keep ordering.

Suppliers, $7.7 million: I am taking the full negotiated saving available on the 30% of supplier spend up for renewal. Suppliers keep their volume, and we pay on the terms we already have.

Wages and hours (workforce), $10.0 million: A temporary reduction of about 4% of remaining payroll, shared across the workforce, rather than layoffs. It sits well below the 10% cap, and it applies to payroll with no roles eliminated.

Eliminating roles, $0: I am not cutting jobs. Severance would cost cash, and the people we would lose are the ones we will need when volumes recover and when we must hire back against the retraining cost of $15,000 per person.

Research and development, $0: R&D funds the product and controls work that will drive future revenue. Cutting the engineering team would be the most damaging long-run choice.

Environmental projects, $0: The energy and emissions projects protect the communities near our plants and lower our costs over time. I will not cut them.

Lower operating income (shareholders), $64.4 million: Shareholders bear the largest remaining share. This is the honest cost of protecting employees, R&D, and the environment. The board sets dividends and repurchases separately; I recommend it weigh that the operating shortfall is being absorbed here.

The cash position remains adequate, with the $300 million undrawn facility available as a backstop.

The $112.1 million shortfall is spread across stakeholders rather than loaded onto any one group.

Shareholders bear the largest share, $54.4 million of lower operating income. They hold the residual risk, and the Company's payout of 90% of earnings can absorb a downturn in the coming year, though the board must decide that separately.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through renegotiated prices. Suppliers face the same volume decline, and this is the full negotiating limit, so I expect pushback and will work with key suppliers on timing and terms.

Customers bear $10.0 million through a price increase of roughly 0.7%, well short of the 3.5% they would accept. Holding back protects volume in a weak market, where a larger increase could cost more than it gains.

The workforce bears $40.0 million. I propose $30.0 million from eliminating roughly 130 roles, weighted to management and non-plant functions, and to be executed mainly through attrition and hiring freezes rather than plant-floor layoffs. Severance will be paid from cash. I also propose a $10.0 million reduction in wages or hours, applied to the remaining payroll, to be shared across the workforce and sized below the 10% maximum. Plant hiring should stop, and affected staff should be considered first for the plant roles the Company routinely fills by retraining.

I will not cut research and development or environmental projects. Those budgets protect future products and the communities near our plants, and cutting them would shift the cost onto stakeholders who had no part in the downturn.

Plant 6, which lost $9.0 million, should be reviewed for consolidation or repositioning. That is a separate decision, but it is the largest structural lever available beyond this year's shortfall.

I will report progress quarterly against these amounts.
